paragraphs.heading: Where we take our questions
paragraphs.edited: We go to places like Google, YouTube and other search engines regularly to find answers to questions like, where's a good restaurant to eat at? How do you fix a bike? And to track down the most recent gossip on a popular celebrity. But an important question is, why do we go there with our questions? I think the answer is because we believe, at least generally, that we'll find helpful, reliable answers to our questions. In 1 Peter 3:15, the Apostle Peter says to sanctify Christ as Lord in our hearts, to always be ready with an answer for the hope within, and to give it with gentleness and give it with respect.

paragraphs.heading: Sitting in the hot seat
paragraphs.edited: While Christians were reading it I was getting a good response, but I started to think to myself, how could I get other non-believers to read it and engage with the ideas? So I called up one of the largest skeptic groups near where I live. I told the head of it, I said, I'd be happy to come sit in the hot seat of your group and just answer questions that you and some of the other skeptics in your group would have toward a Christian. I went up there and they had questions about the existence of God, questions about the Bible, political questions, and even specific questions about what I believed about the soul. It was a blast.

paragraphs.edited: Before the event began, I'd asked the leader if it was okay, toward the end, if I could ask them some questions. Now, I could have asked this group of skeptics how they explain the origin of information in DNA, or the origin of the universe, or how they explain the evidence for the resurrection of Jesus. While those are great questions, I decided to take a different approach. Instead, I asked questions like: what blind spots do Christians have? What bad impressions do Christians often leave? And how can Christians improve their interaction with skeptics?

paragraphs.heading: Grace and truth
paragraphs.edited: You see, the Bible tells us that Jesus came in grace and he came in truth. He came in grace, which is in a loving relationship, and he also spoke truth. We are called to speak truth. We can't compromise truth, but we must do it in love. If we mess up the relationship, so often people won't even hear what we believe is true. If we want people to ask us questions about our faith, we need to be living the kind of lives that invite inquiry. We need to be living the kind of lives that make people wonder, what is the source of that person's hope? But we also need to be ready with some thoughtful questions we can ask other people to help them along on their spiritual journeys.

paragraphs.heading: Four questions worth asking
paragraphs.edited: Here are some specific questions that I've found helpful in my own experience and relationships. First, what do you believe? It's important to find out what the other person believes. Proverbs 18:13 says it is foolish and shameful to answer before you hear. To have an honest conversation with somebody, we first have to understand what that person really believes, and that person is only going to share what they believe when we ask good questions and really listen. Second, why do you believe it?

Proverbs 20 verse 5 says that the purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but it takes a person of understanding who can draw it out. In other words, people have deep reasons for why they believe as they do, and sometimes people know those reasons and sometimes they don't.

paragraphs.edited: Take my father, for example. Before he became a Christian he was an angry agnostic. He looked for ways to shoot Christians down and prove that they were wrong. One thing he didn't fully realize at the time is that he would hear people talk about a Heavenly Father and he thought, why would I want a Heavenly Father? That idea turned him off. Why? Because his earthly father was abusive and absent. His relationship with his father was a deep reason that gave him some anger against God. People have deep reasons for why they believe as they do, and it takes wisdom and listening and patience to help draw out what those real reasons often are.

When we find common ground, often someone's guard will go down and they'll listen in a way they wouldn't have listened before. When I was meeting with these skeptics, they were surprised to find out, even though we clearly differ on a number of significant issues, how much we actually have in common.

paragraphs.heading: You are ready
paragraphs.edited: You have learned some powerful lessons in this study, and you are ready for spiritual conversations. Now, I don't think you have to have all the answers. I don't have even close to all the answers. If someone asks you a tough question, just simply say, I don't know, and then go find an answer so you'll know next time. If you're willing to ask good questions, listen to people and stick with people through their journeys, I think you'll be amazed at how God will use you in people's lives to make a difference with them spiritually. Go for it.
